narrative:
The model predicted a 65.1% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the second decile placed you noticeably below the average student who was admitted. Your first-year ranking in the third decile had a similar, though slightly smaller, negative effect. These two performance measures together signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 30 worked in the opposite direction. While it still pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, its helpful effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your lower class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 (versus an average of 3.23 among accepted students), middle family income, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Raising your class standing in future years, retaking the LSAT to boost your score, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. Consider reapplying once you have demonstrated clearer evidence of readiness for the bar.
